problem: Topological navigation methods (e.g., SPTM, GNM/ViNT) typically need environment-specific or large-scale pre-training and training data, and generalize poorly to new environments. Metric SLAM is compute-heavy.
motivation: Topological maps are lightweight and human-like, but building them quickly in unknown environments without training is hard. AnyLoc, a training-free universal VPR method (DINOv2 + VLAD), provides robust image similarity across environments, which can serve as the sole perceptual primitive for mapping, localization and control.
key_idea: Use AnyLoc global-descriptor cosine similarity as the single primitive for keyframe node addition, loop closure, localization, node switching, and left/middle/right image-crop based action control, giving training-free monocular topological mapping and navigation from one walkthrough video.
insight: A single training-free VPR descriptor can replace learned action-prediction and localization modules; versus a ResNet18 action model (trained SPTM-style), it generalizes much better, especially on longer/harder routes and in an unseen office scene (SR 1.00 vs 0.25). The sparsity study shows denser maps are not better: nodes too close cause missed nodes and frequent re-localization, so an appropriate sparsity matters.
method: Similarity via AnyLoc: DINOv2 features aggregated with VLAD into global descriptors; cosine similarity between frames is the universal signal.

Node addition: from video frames, add a new node when similarity to the last node drops below T_add_new_node (distance case) or due to large orientation change (angular case); T_interval sets the minimum spacing.
Relative distance: an edge weight counter increments only when consecutive-frame similarity is below T_add_distance, avoiding increments when stationary.

Loop closure and map optimization: a candidate node whose similarity to an existing node exceeds T_loop_closure is not added; the previous node is linked to the existing one. Thresholds control map sparsity.

Localization and planning: goal image and current observation are matched against node descriptors (threshold T_milestone, rotate counterclockwise if no match); Dijkstra on the directed weighted graph gives the node sequence.
Node selection: switch to next node when similarity to the current node falls below T_change_node and the next node exceeds T_milestone; matching restricted to a window around the current node.

Local motion control: split the image into Left/Middle/Right crops, compare each with the target node image via AnyLoc, and move toward the most similar (above T_limited_control); a two-cycle consistency check smooths actions, allowing forward-left/right combos.

setting.training_data: none (training-free); map built from a single walkthrough video
setting.action_space: discrete forward / left / right / forward-left / forward-right via image-crop similarity
setting.simulator: NVIDIA Isaac Sim (hospital and office scenes, Limo robot with ROS2); plus real-world campus data
setting.privileged: none (a pre-recorded walkthrough video of the environment is used to build the map)

numbers.extra: compared with ResNet18+AnyLoc baseline trained SPTM-style; both use AnyLoc for localization

numbers.eval_set_note: custom route; 14 trials; baseline ResNet model trained in hospital
numbers.extra: unseen office environment; average over the four routes is 0.95

numbers_note: Custom simulation routes in Isaac Sim, not a standard benchmark. Baseline ResNet+AnyLoc: 1.00/0.64/0.47/0.25, average 0.59. Real-world experiments are qualitative only (replayed video, no numbers).
results: The method achieves average SR 0.95 across four simulated routes vs 0.59 for a ResNet18+AnyLoc (SPTM-style) baseline, claimed as a 60.2% average improvement. The gap widens with route length and in the unseen office (1.00 vs 0.25), with no pre-training required.
limitations: Needs manual tuning of many thresholds (T_add_new_node, T_loop_closure, T_milestone, etc.) for mapping and navigation.
Evaluation is small and custom: a few routes with 14 trials in Isaac Sim, one baseline; real-world navigation is a qualitative video replay rather than a real robot run.
Relies on image-similarity only, with no obstacle avoidance or richer cues, and requires a prior walkthrough video.
